# Native memory fixture preparation

This x64 fixture supplies the schema-one buffers and correlated RPC contract used
by the internal memory adapters. It is a separate build artifact from the Python
fixture. Its runtime behavior and native memory acceptance have **not been run**.

The executable requires `--rpc --challenge <32 lowercase hex digits>`.
It uses inherited input/output pipes, a 1,024-byte frame limit, and the closed
`bootstrap`, `snapshot` and `compare_set` operations. Malformed JSON, duplicate or
unknown keys, escaped/non-ASCII strings and oversized frames terminate the stream.
It has no arbitrary memory request, legacy `set`, desktop input or window API.

The payload is a uint32 document ID and a 12-byte zero-padded state. An aligned
64-bit odd/even sequence encloses mutations. The 128-entry operation ledger never
evicts; duplicate requests recover their original result and new IDs are refused
when full. The launch nonce is generated by the Windows cryptographic provider.
Bootstrap PID and locations are still self-reported and require independent checks.

## Fixed page layouts

The optional startup arguments `--page-layout <layout>` select one of four fixed
diagnostic layouts. They accept no address, size, protection value or later mutation.
Each allocates two pages, copies the initial 16-byte payload across their boundary
(eight bytes in each), and keeps the header and sequence in separate static storage.

| Layout | First page | Second page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `split` | Read-only | Read/write |
| `guard` | Read-only | Read/write with guard |
| `noaccess` | Read-only | No access |
| `decommitted` | Read-only | Reserved, decommitted |

Different readable protections in `split` prevent the two pages from forming one
query region. Other layouts prepare reader refusals. All diagnostic modes allow
bootstrap only and reject every control request before accessing the copied data.
The ordinary mode continues to use its original static payload and command ledger.
Every exit path attempts to release the original allocation, including initialization
and stdio failures; a failed release returns exit code 3.

These layouts have been compiled and source-reviewed, not executed. The CLI below
can select one with `--page-layout <layout>`. Selection alone remains static;
execution still requires `--execute` after the native pause is lifted.

The page runner binds its private payload address only after launch/bootstrap
validation. It observes the reader's existing region queries without adding OS
calls, and requires both exact pages on one retained handle. The first page must
be readable and read-only, end at the payload midpoint, and supply a successful
eight-byte prefix read before the second page is queried. The second page must
share the allocation and match the requested protection and commitment state.
Metadata changes invalidate the evidence even if the original mapping returns.
Multiple observations cannot contribute to one successful page result.
Each runner claims a fresh evidence scope before observing and consumes it once;
an earlier successful trace cannot be replayed against a different target.

`split` also requires document 17, state `ready`, revision zero. Other layouts
require `unreadable_region` from a read with matching payload-page evidence and no
read of the protected second half. The same error from an image, header or sequence
page cannot satisfy the case. Reports expose only the requested layout and closed
check booleans, never the private locations or memory contents. Page cases issue no
state-changing control command. They require the expected read-only IPC snapshot
and do not claim runtime task completion. The overall fault matrix
stays unverified; only injected tests have exercised this runner so far.

The allocation and protection rules follow Microsoft's
[VirtualProtect](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/memoryapi/nf-memoryapi-virtualprotect)
and [VirtualFree](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/memoryapi/nf-memoryapi-virtualfree)
contracts. Guard pages are a
[one-shot access alarm](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/memory/creating-guard-pages);
the fixture does not access the protected copy after setup.

## Build without execution

Build only with the installed x64 MSVC and Windows SDK, supplying their versioned
roots and a **new** output directory:

```powershell
.venv/Scripts/python.exe test/fixtures/native_memory/build_fixture.py `
  --msvc '<MSVC version directory>' --sdk '<Windows Kits/10 directory>' `
  --sdk-version '<SDK version>' --output '<new build directory>'
```

The builder copies the source, clears ambient compiler/linker options, and compiles
with `/MT /W4 /WX /O2 /GS /guard:cf`. It checks that the copy did not change during
the build. It then runs `dumpbin`, **not the fixture**, to require an x64 image whose
direct DLL imports are exactly `bcrypt.dll` and `kernel32.dll`.

The output includes the source copy, object, executable, compiler log, static image
report and a manifest binding the source, image, compiler and inspector hashes.
This is a build inventory, not a trusted-build certificate. It does not verify OS
DLL resolution, loaded executable bytes, foreground noninterference or runtime
behavior. Each build has its own image hash; reproducibility is not claimed.
The manifest records execution, dependency trust and acceptance as unverified.

Do not register this artifact as a supported target or execute it as part of
ordinary tests. Native execution remains subject to the explicit pause in
`Progress.md`. Loaded-image comparison, trusted dependency binding and the native
fault acceptance remain separate requirements.

Put the build directory somewhere only you and administrators can change, such as a
new folder under `%LOCALAPPDATA%`. Before launching, the image lease refuses a path
with a junction in it or with any directory another account may rename, delete or
add files to, so a secondary drive root granting Authenticated Users Modify, or a
`%TEMP%` shared with other accounts, cannot hold a fixture that will run.

## Prepare the smoke check

From the repository root, use the checkout's modules rather than a separately
installed AutoControl version:

```powershell
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -c "import runpy; runpy.run_path('test/fixtures/native_memory/acceptance.py', run_name='__main__')" `
  --build '<build directory>' --sha256 '<independently reviewed executable hash>'
```

This default command only reads bounded files. It matches the image against the
external pin, checks the build inventory and source snapshot, and parses the PE
plan. Source inventory matching does not prove how the binary was compiled.
The report must say `execution=not_run`; the build manifest is never rewritten.

After the user explicitly resumes native acceptance, the same command's
`--execute` option runs one owned fixture. Do not use that option while the pause
in `Progress.md` remains active. It verifies the initial state, sends one grounded
command, checks a fresh semantic readback, and checks runtime completion. Cleanup
tries runtime, target and temporary-directory retirement independently, with one
retry for failed cleanup only. It never retries the command. Cancellation and
hard interruption propagate after cleanup; no success JSON is emitted for them.

The diagnostic selects a 60-second read ceiling and a 60-second action ceiling,
within the existing allowed limits, to include repeated live policy checkpoints.
These are diagnostic ceilings, not performance targets; ordinary target defaults
remain unchanged. The report exposes the read ceiling and each completed check.
An ordinary failure yields a fixed category or reader failure code, never an
exception message, address, nonce or bootstrap packet.

Even `execution=passed` means only this smoke path passed. Dependency trust,
foreground noninterference, page faults, PID reuse, permissions, architecture
coverage, resource growth and full native acceptance remain unverified. A cleanup
failure keeps the run failed even when the retry retires the resources. This
script is not registered as a supported production target or included in ordinary
native test execution.

## UI observation fixture, build only

The builder accepts `--kind uia` for the separate `uia_fixture.c` source and
`uia_fixture.exe` image. The default remains `--kind memory`. UIA builds require
exactly kernel32/user32 imports and publish a schema-2 manifest with `fixture_kind`
and `executable`; the memory acceptance runner refuses this artifact. No builder
path runs either executable.

The UI fixture accepts only `--challenge <32 lowercase hex digits>`. A dedicated
thread creates a parent without `WS_VISIBLE`, with `WS_EX_NOACTIVATE` and
`WS_EX_TOOLWINDOW`, at off-screen coordinates. It never calls ShowWindow, focus
or foreground APIs. The same thread creates, pumps and destroys these read-only
EDIT controls:

| Child ID | Fixture value / purpose |
| --- | --- |
| 1001 | `17`, document value |
| 1002 | `ready`, status value |
| 1003 | Empty string |
| 1004 | `disabled`, disabled control |
| 1005 | Password-style control containing synthetic fixture text |
| 1006, twice | Different values to test ambiguous selection |

Both inherited stdin and stdout must be pipes. After initialization, stdout emits
one JSON line with exactly `id` and `result`. The ID is the launch challenge;
result contains exactly `fixture`, `version`, `pid`, `hwnd` and `challenge`.
These private bootstrap claims still
require retained-process and window-owner validation. No control values are sent
through stdout. Closing stdin requests shutdown; any input byte also stops the
fixture with a protocol error. A separate pipe waiter lets the owner also observe
unexpected GUI-thread exit; window destruction posts quit to that thread.
Startup and thread shutdown waits are five
seconds; failed retirement exits the entire process with code 3. The parent must
retain process ownership and enforce its own deadline, including blocked pipe I/O.
The internal launcher uses `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` for this console-subsystem image.

The event-aware pump follows
[MsgWaitForMultipleObjects](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-msgwaitformultipleobjects).
The parent styles follow Microsoft's
[extended-window-style contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winmsg/extended-window-styles).
Child IDs do not prove UIA AutomationId mapping or hidden-control exposure.
Those properties, password behavior, cleanup and foreground noninterference remain
unverified until native acceptance resumes. The internal `OwnedUiaLauncher` consumes that bootstrap through a receive-only
owned channel. It rechecks process facts through the retained launch handle and
the window owner through GetWindowThreadProcessId. Injected native calls and hidden
Python helpers cover this binding, not native HWND behavior. The scoped UIA reader,
managed assembly and per-field report results remain pending in Progress.md.
